Question: What does it mean when a Google interviewer says, “There is no feedback on this one” after an interview question?
Old_Answer: After an interview, interviewers are required to give detailed feedback according to several criteria. However, over all the time that the interviewer and candidate interact, there are periods when candidates are not judged, roughly the first 5 minutes and the last 5. It can be difficult to detect when the interview time proper actually starts, versus when the interviewer is still trying to build rapport. Likewise, candidates can feel that they are being evaluated as they ask questions, and feel forced to pick questions as a last opportunity to score points versus as a chance to get a candid answer on something they want to know. So, some interviewers like to signal when the candidate is “off the hook”. If a candidate says or does something completely outrageous during that time, the interviewer will still have to report it, but the bar for outrageous is pretty high, like: personal attacks.
Answer_with_writing_sample: When a Google interviewer says, “There is no feedback on this one” after an interview question, it can be a bit disheartening, but it’s important to understand the context. This phrase typically indicates that the interviewer is either unable to provide specific feedback due to company policy or that the question was designed to gauge your thought process rather than to elicit a definitive answer. In many cases, interviewers are looking for how you approach problems, your reasoning, and your ability to communicate your thoughts clearly. The lack of feedback doesn’t necessarily mean you performed poorly; it may simply reflect the nature of the question or the interview process itself. It’s also worth noting that Google’s interview structure is often standardized, and interviewers may not have the flexibility to give detailed feedback on every question. Instead of dwelling on the absence of feedback, focus on what you can control: your preparation and performance. Reflect on your answers and the thought process you used during the interview. If you felt confident in your reasoning and approach, that’s a positive takeaway. Remember, interviews are as much about fit as they are about skills, and sometimes the feedback is simply that you didn’t align with what they were looking for at that moment. Use this experience as a learning opportunity for future interviews, and keep honing your skills and understanding of the interview process.

It is quite an achievement to be promoted to that level, and that’s something that happens usually between 5 to 8 years after being hired. It’s really up to any organization to determine where to draw the line between junior and senior and what level of experience represents the pivot. Question: How do you interview for software engineering positions when the candidate has no prior experience in the field?
Old_Answer: How would I interview a candidate who has no industry experience, exactly like a candidate who does. They would get the same coding tests and the same behavioral interviews. A lot of the professional experience of a candidate can be used for these behavioral interviews regardless of their actual role. How would I prepare as a candidate had I no experience as a software engineer, well, how I’ve done it when I interviewed as a software engineer from another career. I prepared for the coding test until I felt I was ready. There’s ample material available, much more than when I made that career change. Candidates won’t get a pass just because they had a different job title before, but they also get a shot at it even though they don’t necessarily come from a software engineering background.
Answer_with_writing_sample: Interviewing candidates for software engineering positions who lack prior experience can be challenging, but it’s also an opportunity to identify potential and aptitude. First, focus on assessing their foundational knowledge and problem-solving skills. This can be done through technical questions that cover basic programming concepts, algorithms, and data structures. Even without experience, a candidate should be able to demonstrate an understanding of these fundamentals. Additionally, consider their ability to learn and adapt; ask about projects they've worked on during their education or personal time, even if they are not professional experiences. This can provide insight into their passion for the field and their initiative to learn independently. Behavioral questions are also crucial; inquire about their teamwork, communication skills, and how they handle challenges. These soft skills can often be just as important as technical abilities, especially for entry-level positions. Furthermore, consider incorporating a practical coding exercise or a take-home project that allows candidates to showcase their skills in a real-world scenario. This not only evaluates their coding abilities but also their approach to problem-solving and creativity. Lastly, remember that potential is key; look for candidates who show enthusiasm for learning and a willingness to grow within the role. While they may not have direct experience, their attitude and aptitude can often outweigh the lack of a traditional background in software engineering.

Question: How should an interview with a software developer be concluded if it is clear that the candidate will not be hired?
Old_Answer: Let’s step out of the interview room a little bit. Candidate Alice interviews for BigTech co. The next day, she meets Bob for coffee. How are you, asks Bob. Well, I interviewed for BigTech co yesterday, says Alice. So, how was it? wonders Bob. The interview experience is designed, so that we can influence what Alice will say next. “Oh, they were really super nice, but I don’t think I am going to pass. Too bad, because it looked really cool. “ Or “I don’t care, they’re pompous assholes, I won’t take an offer no matter with how many 0s. “ Candidates talk far and wide about their interviewing experience, so a positive or negative experience can have a profound impact on the employer brand. This should inform how to talk to candidates, regardless of their performance.
Answer_with_writing_sample: Concluding an interview with a software developer when it’s clear they won’t be hired can be a delicate task. It’s essential to approach this situation with empathy and professionalism. First, it’s important to provide constructive feedback, if appropriate. This can help the candidate understand the areas where they fell short, whether it was technical skills, problem-solving abilities, or cultural fit. However, be cautious not to overwhelm them with too much information; focus on one or two key points that could aid their future interviews. Next, express gratitude for their time and effort in the interview process. A simple acknowledgment of their interest in the position and the company can go a long way in softening the blow of rejection. It’s also beneficial to leave the door open for future opportunities. You might say something like, “While we won’t be moving forward at this time, we encourage you to apply for future openings that align more closely with your skills.” This not only maintains a positive relationship but also encourages the candidate to keep the company in mind for future roles. Finally, ensure that the candidate knows they can reach out for any further questions or clarification. This gesture reinforces a respectful and supportive atmosphere, which is crucial in maintaining a positive employer brand, even in rejection.
Answer_with_user_profile: Concluding an interview with a software developer, especially when it's clear that the candidate will not be hired, requires a delicate balance of professionalism and empathy. First and foremost, it’s essential to maintain a respectful tone throughout the conversation. Begin by thanking the candidate for their time and effort in preparing for the interview. Acknowledge the skills they demonstrated and any relevant experiences they shared, as this helps to soften the blow of the rejection. It’s also beneficial to provide constructive feedback, focusing on specific areas where they could improve or skills that may be lacking for the role in question. This not only helps the candidate grow but also shows that you value their potential. If appropriate, you might suggest resources or avenues for further development, which can leave them with a sense of direction. Finally, it’s important to encourage them to apply for future openings, as this maintains a positive relationship and reflects well on your company’s culture. Ending on a hopeful note can make a significant difference in how the candidate perceives the experience, turning what could be a disappointing moment into an opportunity for growth. Remember, the way you conclude the interview can influence the candidate's perception of your organization, so strive to leave them with a sense of respect and encouragement, even if the outcome isn’t what they hoped for.
Answer_with_full_information: Concluding an interview with a software developer when it’s clear they won’t be hired is a delicate task that requires empathy and professionalism. First and foremost, it’s essential to provide constructive feedback. This not only helps the candidate understand areas for improvement but also shows that their time and effort were valued. For instance, if the candidate struggled with technical questions, you might say, “While your enthusiasm is commendable, we noticed some gaps in your technical knowledge that we typically expect for this role.” This approach maintains respect and dignity, allowing the candidate to leave with a sense of purpose rather than disappointment. Additionally, it’s crucial to communicate the decision clearly but kindly. You might say something like, “After careful consideration, we’ve decided to move forward with other candidates who more closely match our current needs.” This transparency helps manage expectations and avoids leaving the candidate in limbo. This not only softens the blow but also reinforces a positive image of your company as one that cares about the growth of individuals in the tech community. Ultimately, the goal is to ensure that the candidate leaves the interview feeling respected and informed, even if the outcome isn’t what they hoped for.

Question: What is the process for someone with no college education to work as a software engineer at Google or Facebook? How long does this take?
Old_Answer: Education gives a leg up for candidates because Google and Meta are actively recruiting in certain campuses. The easiest way is to get an internship and convert it into an offer. But in the general case, you get hired by passing an interview, which takes 2 steps: being invited to interview, and performing well at the interview. Anyone can succeed in step 2 regardless of education as long as they have the skills, and anyone who has the disposition can learn the skills. When you don’t have a degree, it is step 1 which is harder. When I was working at Facebook, I had 2 teammates that didn’t have a college degree. Prior to Facebook, one was a key contributor to an influential open source library, and the other had already a resume more impressive than most people twice his age, having started a sold a business. In my personal case, I had a degree, just not in computer science. But what I had was a well-read blog. This helped enter the hiring pipeline.

Old_Answer: As someone who has spent a lot of time using Quora and understanding Google Search, I believe I can give a decent answer to this question. When you think of search engines of the 90s, you have that search box where a user is going to enter text, and then after they submit the search, they are going to get a series of links that contain the text searched. This is not how modern search engines work (Google or otherwise). Today, what people enter in the search box is less a phrase to look for in a vast pile of documents, and more a command. Users expect to get something relevant in response to that command. Technically, what people put in the search box is called a query. The first thing the search engine is going to do, “understanding”, is to extract an intent from the query. An intent is a formal representation of what the user wants. To take the quintessential example of Google if a user types “obama height” they do not want to find all the documents that contain the phrase obama height, but most likely want to know how tall Barack Obama is. Extracting an intent is not enough. There are hundreds of servlets which are treating a query and which are either detecting an intent in a query or assigning metadata to the query, such as: how polite is the tone, as this yields different results. So typically, many intents are extracted. Next the search engine is going to rank these intents. Sometimes one intent is overwhelmingly likely, and it’s very unlikely that the user actually meant something else. Sometimes, it’s not as clear cut. So in our example, maybe the user wanted the height of Michelle Obama. Maybe by some logic they wanted to know Trump’s or Biden’s. And maybe, you know what, they wanted to see webpages that talk about “height” and “obama”. OK, so now Google has several intents ranked. What to do next is fulfillment and execution. Fulfillment means that it’s going to prepare answers corresponding to all the intents. Execution means it’s going to actually get those answers from the servers and render them on screen, and is not super relevant for this question. In the case of “obama height”, in google’s parliance there are a couple of intents which are going to be fulfilled, one is “knowledge base lookup” and one is “web search”. Knowledge base lookup means that the user is looking for a well-known facet (“height”) of an well-known entity (“former US president Barack Obama”) is Google’s representation of the world, its knowledge base. BTW the answer is 6′2″, a fact which is drilled into the mind of anyone who works or has worked in Google Search. When there is a “hit” for knowledge base, or really for any of the intents it understands, then Google is going to answer to the intent with a special card. That’s the happy path because if Google actually guessed the intent of the user, then the special card is going to do a much better job at responding to it than expecting them to click on one of 10 blue links. But web search is almost always fired as well, which is the list of blue links with a blurb. So on to Quora content. Quora is used by Google’s knowledge base as one of many trusted sources of information. This doesn’t mean that Google feels that whatever is in a Quora answer is absolute truth. But there is some curation, there is some validation by other users through upvotes and downvotes, so it’s much better than an arbitrary piece of web content. That is not foolproof. A notorious example is when some folks decided to update the height of cartoon character Caillou on the Fandom wiki (another trusted source, due to its human curation). Caillou, a toddler, still comes up as being 5′11″ if you google “caillou height”. Google is well aware that “it happens” and generally doesn’t care as long as directionally, content from trusted sources is more reliable on average. It also has mechanisms to address poor results. As a user you can report an answer as poor (and as a human you can also try to tweak the source of the knowledge base which I suspect is still going on with Caillou). So the answer of your question is that for the queries for which there are Quora answer, Google doesn’t have more authoritative content and it believes it is more useful to the user than just sending them to a list of links. Google also found that more often than not, when displayed, Quora content is actually helpful.

Question: What is the reason for the high number of failures in technical interviews at Google and Facebook? Is it due to lack of preparation from candidates, or is there another reason?
Old_Answer: Google gets about 3 million applications per year. There are very few open positions. That’s all you need to know. During a big part of the 2010s, the reasoning behind tech hiring is that someone who is good enough should get a job. This may still be true in some companies that are in very fast growth. In most of the tech world though, candidates are applying for a specific role in a specific team, so there will be a limited number of candidates who will get an offer. This allows employers to move the bar up. So sure, there is a lot of advice out there for candidates, and a lot of it makes sense. But there is no such thing as “the most common mistake” which if addressed will guarantee a spot. At the end of the day, interviews are complex human interactions with a lot of variables in play, evaluations are subjective to some extent, hiring committee is also composed of humans and there are lots of factors that contribute to a decision.
Answer_with_writing_sample: The high number of failures in technical interviews at Google and Facebook can often be attributed to a combination of factors, with lack of preparation being a significant one. Many candidates underestimate the complexity and rigor of these interviews, thinking that their existing experience will suffice. However, the interview process is designed to assess not only technical skills but also problem-solving abilities and cultural fit. Candidates frequently fall into the trap of believing they can "wing it," which is a risky approach given the competitive nature of these roles. Moreover, the interview format often includes algorithmic challenges and system design questions that require a deep understanding of concepts, which many candidates may not have fully grasped. Additionally, the pressure of the interview environment can lead to performance anxiety, causing even well-prepared candidates to falter. Another factor is the mismatch between the candidate's experience and the expectations of the role; many applicants may not have the specific skills or knowledge that the interviewers are looking for. Ultimately, while preparation is crucial, candidates also need to align their skills with the job requirements and practice under realistic conditions to improve their chances of success. It’s a multifaceted issue, and understanding this can help candidates approach their preparation more strategically.

Answer_with_writing_sample: Walking into major tech companies like Apple or Google and asking for a job might seem like a straightforward approach, but the reality is much more complex. First, these companies have structured hiring processes that involve multiple stages, including resume screenings, technical assessments, and interviews with various stakeholders. Simply walking in bypasses these essential steps, which are designed to ensure that candidates meet specific qualifications and cultural fit. Additionally, tech companies receive thousands of applications daily, making it impractical for hiring managers to entertain walk-in inquiries. Moreover, the tech industry places a significant emphasis on networking and referrals; candidates who have connections within the company often have a better chance of getting noticed. This means that building relationships and leveraging professional networks can be more effective than a spontaneous visit. Lastly, the nature of the roles at these companies often requires specialized skills and experience, which are evaluated through rigorous interview processes. Therefore, while the idea of walking in and asking for a job may seem appealing, it overlooks the structured and competitive nature of tech hiring, where preparation, networking, and understanding the application process are key to success.
